title: Implement and manage human resource and labour relations policies and acts

lessons.title: The labour law framework for farms
lessons.html:
Laws every farm manager must know

South African labour law applies fully to agriculture. Managers who understand it avoid costly disputes, build trust and run a more productive workforce.

LawMain content
Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995 (LRA)Fair dismissal, unfair labour practices, unions, strikes, the CCMA and bargaining
Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997 (BCEA)Working hours, overtime, leave, notice, payslips, contracts
Sectoral Determination 13: Farm Worker SectorSpecific conditions for farm workers under the BCEA
National Minimum Wage Act 9 of 2018The national minimum wage, adjusted periodically
Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998Prohibits unfair discrimination; affirmative action for designated employers
Skills Development Act 97 of 1998Workplace skills planning, SETAs (AgriSETA for agriculture)
Unemployment Insurance Act 63 of 2001UIF registration and contributions
Compensation for Occupational Injuries and Diseases Act 130 of 1993 (COIDA)Compensation for work injuries and diseases
OHS Act 85 of 1993Health and safety in the workplace
Extension of Security of Tenure Act 62 of 1997 (ESTA)Rights of occupiers living on farms; lawful eviction procedures

Keeping up to date

Minimum wage rates and some conditions change regularly. Check the Department of Employment and Labour's current notices rather than relying on memory, and get advice from an agricultural employers' organisation or labour lawyer for complex matters.

Why compliance matters

Non-compliance can lead to inspections, compliance orders, back-pay claims, CCMA awards and reputational damage with buyers who audit ethical trade. Good compliance is also simply fair treatment of the people who make the farm work.

lessons.title: HR policies and procedures
lessons.html:
Turning law into farm policy

Policies translate laws into clear rules for the farm. They must be written, explained to workers in a language they understand, and applied consistently.

Essential HR policies

  • Recruitment and selection: fair, non-discriminatory, based on job requirements.
  • Employment contracts: written particulars of employment as the BCEA requires, including job, pay, hours, leave and notice.
  • Working time and leave: hours, overtime, Sunday and public holiday work, annual, sick, family responsibility and maternity or parental leave.
  • Remuneration: pay at least the applicable minimum wage, lawful deductions only, and itemised payslips.
  • Disciplinary code and procedure based on the LRA Code of Good Practice: Dismissal.
  • Grievance procedure so workers can raise problems.
  • Health and safety policy under the OHS Act.
  • Housing policy where workers live on the farm, consistent with ESTA.
  • Harassment and anti-discrimination policy.
  • Training and development linked to a workplace skills plan.

Seasonal and contract workers

Seasonal pickers and packers have the same basic rights as permanent workers for the period they work. If labour brokers are used, the farm can share responsibility for compliance, so check the broker's registration, UIF and COIDA status and pay practices.

Record keeping

Keep records of time worked, pay, leave, contracts, disciplinary actions and training for the periods the law requires. Accurate records are your best defence in any dispute.

Communication

Hold regular meetings with workers or their representatives. Explain changes before they happen. Many disputes start with misunderstanding rather than bad intent.

lessons.title: Managing labour relations, discipline and disputes
lessons.html:
Fairness in practice

Discipline

Discipline aims to correct behaviour, not punish. The LRA requires dismissals to be both substantively fair (a fair reason: misconduct, incapacity or operational requirements) and procedurally fair (a fair process).

  1. Investigate the facts.
  2. Notify the worker of the allegation in writing in a language they understand.
  3. Give reasonable time to prepare and allow a representative (fellow worker or union representative).
  4. Hold a hearing where the worker can respond and call witnesses.
  5. Decide on the evidence and consider the worker's record and circumstances.
  6. Communicate the outcome and the right to refer a dispute to the CCMA.

Progressive discipline (verbal warning, written warning, final written warning) is appropriate for less serious misconduct. Serious misconduct such as theft, assault or gross negligence endangering lives may justify dismissal after a fair hearing.

Incapacity and retrenchment

Poor performance and ill health require counselling, support and reasonable accommodation before dismissal. Retrenchment for operational reasons (for example drought or mechanisation) requires consultation under the LRA on alternatives, selection criteria and severance.

Unions and collective relations

Workers have the right to join a union. Managers must not victimise union members. Build a working relationship with recognised unions and worker committees.

Disputes

Most disputes go to the CCMA for conciliation, then arbitration or the Labour Court. Handle grievances early to prevent escalation.

Key points

  • Know the main labour laws: LRA, BCEA, minimum wage, EEA, SDA, UIF, COIDA, OHS and ESTA.
  • Write and explain clear HR policies and apply them consistently.
  • Dismissals must be substantively and procedurally fair.
  • Consult properly before retrenchment.
  • Keep accurate records and resolve grievances early.
